#6419. Scientists Find That Mice, Not Deer, Hold a Major Clue to Lyme Disease Risk

A 35-year study reveals that mice, acorns, and unexpected environmental forces hold surprising clues to predicting Lyme disease risk. A remarkable 35-year study is challenging long-held assumptions about Lyme disease, revealing that mice, acorns, and even extreme weather influence tick populations in unexpected ways. One of the biggest surprises is that deer, often associated with the spread of Lyme disease, may be less important in predicting the numbers of dangerous ticks than researchers once believed.

Diseases transmitted by ticks are becoming increasingly common across the United States. Lyme disease is the most frequently reported, with nearly 500,000 people diagnosed annually. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through bites from infected blacklegged ticks. Antibiotics can successfully treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may spread to the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have investigated the complicated relationships among oak trees, acorns, rodents, predators, ticks, and climate. Their goal has been to understand how these interconnected factors influence the risk of Lyme disease in humans.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences highlights nine particularly unexpected discoveries from this decades-long research effort. Several findings challenge conventional thinking about how tick populations grow and what determines the likelihood of disease transmission.

“On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the unusually extensive dataset has been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from random fluctuations and misleading correlations. Relationships that seem convincing over a few years can look very different when examined across several decades.

“Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare,” said LaDeau. “This research has followed an ecological community — including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms — examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study.”

When scientists first identified Lyme disease in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely factor in the disease’s spread. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying large numbers of adult ticks, suggesting that deer populations might strongly influence how many ticks would emerge in subsequent seasons.

Deer do not directly transmit the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks. However, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks, allowing those ticks to reproduce. Researchers therefore suspected that larger deer populations would support more egg-laying females and ultimately produce more young ticks.

Decades of field observations have complicated that theory. At the Cary Institute’s 2,000-acre forested research site in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant relationship between deer abundance and the number of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks and represent the life stage most likely to transmit Lyme disease to humans.

“We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data,” said Ostfeld, “but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing.”

Although deer numbers did not reliably predict nymph populations, mouse numbers told a different story.

The researchers discovered that years with abundant mice were followed by an approximately 40% increase in nymphal ticks the next year. This relationship makes white-footed mice particularly important to understanding changes in tick populations.

These small rodents provide an excellent food source for blacklegged tick larvae. They are also highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to the young ticks feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can carry the bacteria into their next developmental stage. When they feed again as nymphs, they can transmit the infection to humans.

One of the study’s most striking discoveries involves something seemingly unrelated to human disease: acorns.

Oak trees occasionally produce unusually large quantities of acorns in a synchronized event known as acorn masting. The sudden abundance of food benefits mice, allowing their populations to increase during the following year.

That population boom then provides more feeding opportunities for young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly large acorn harvest can reliably predict increased numbers of nymphal ticks two years later.

This creates a remarkable ecological chain reaction in which events beginning in the forest canopy can influence tick populations years afterward.

The relationship between mice and Lyme disease produced another unexpected finding.

Because mice are so effective at transmitting B. burgdorferi, the scientists initially assumed that years with more mice would also have a higher percentage of infected nymphal ticks. Early observations appeared to support that prediction.

However, the connection gradually disappeared as the research team accumulated more years of data.

“It kept me up at night,” said Ostfeld, “because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.”

Further investigation pointed toward a more complicated explanation involving other animals that provide blood meals for ticks.

When mouse populations increase, populations of other potential hosts, including squirrels, skunks, and opossums, may also rise. Most of these animals are much less effective at transmitting the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks.

Consequently, a greater share of ticks feeding on these alternative hosts can reduce the overall percentage of infected nymphs, even when mice are plentiful.

“So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts,” explained Ostfeld. “It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case.”

The findings demonstrate why predicting the total number of ticks is different from predicting how many of those ticks carry Lyme disease.

Another surprise emerged when the researchers compared laboratory experiments with conditions in the wild.

Previous laboratory studies had suggested that extreme heat and severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that the insects were far more resilient than expected.

The researchers suspect that ticks escape dangerous temperatures by moving deeper into the soil or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less extreme.

However, temperature still appears to influence tick populations in important ways. The team found that years with generally warmer conditions tended to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual.

This creates an intriguing contradiction. Warmer years typically benefit mice, which should help support larger tick populations, yet the researchers have not observed a corresponding overall increase in nymphs.

Understanding how these opposing effects interact remains an important focus of the ongoing research.

Together, the discoveries suggest that Lyme disease risk is shaped by a complicated network of ecological relationships, but one that contains patterns scientists can use to make predictions.

The strong connection between mouse abundance and future tick numbers could help public health officials anticipate periods of elevated risk. Likewise, recognizing that deer abundance is not a reliable predictor of nymph populations at the study site, and that severe winter weather may not substantially reduce tick numbers, could improve disease prevention strategies.

Important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will influence the relationships among ticks, rodents, oak trees, and other wildlife.

“You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far,” said Ostfeld. “We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it’s very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production.”

Since the monitoring program began in 1991, its research site in Dutchess County has undergone numerous environmental changes, including shifting climate conditions, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species.

The scientists intend to continue tracking how ticks and the animals they depend on respond to these changes. By extending an already exceptional research record, they hope to uncover more of the hidden ecological patterns that could help predict Lyme disease risk and protect human health in the years ahead.

Reference: “The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis” by Richard S. Ostfeld, Shannon L. LaDeau, Kelly Oggenfuss, Charles D. Canham, Michael Fargione, Raymond J. Winchcombe and Felicia Keesing, 17 August 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2610907123

Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria.

According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus, repeated that story without question.

But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die?

Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery.

"We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones, a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email.

What historians largely agree on is that Cleopatra VII, the last queen of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, took her own life and that she chose a method that left her body composed and dignified.

Physical evidence of Cleopatra's death is elusive. Much of Alexandria's royal quarter now lies underwater, and underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, who has been excavating it, hasn't found the queen's mausoleum, Jones said. Even if Cleopatra's remains surfaced, bones would be unlikely to show evidence of snake venom, she added, noting that forensics is outside her area of expertise.

Divers celebrate as a crane pulls an artifact from the waters at Abu Qir bay in Alexandria, Egypt on Aug. 21, 2025.

The best witness may have been Olympus, Cleopatra's personal physician. "Unfortunately, nothing survives of Olympus' account," Jones said.

What does remain is a story told largely by Cleopatra's enemies. The earliest surviving account is a poem by the Roman poet Horace, whose patron was a close friend of Octavian, said Jane Draycott, a historian at the University of Glasgow. His Ode 1.37, written around the time of her death, celebrates Octavian's victory and already pictures the queen handling serpents — yet it ends with grudging admiration for a woman who refused to be paraded as a trophy.

Following her capture, Cleopatra was held under military guard. By then, she had already tried to end her life twice. Cleopatra had tried to stab herself when Roman soldiers broke into the mausoleum where she had barricaded herself, and she later tried to starve herself, stopping only after Octavian threatened her children.

To Draycott, those attempts leave little doubt that Cleopatra would rather die than live as a captive. "She does not want to be a prisoner; she does not want to be led through the streets of Rome in triumph as a defeated foe," she told Live Science.

In the Greco-Roman world, suicide didn't carry the stigma it later acquired under Christianity, she added. "It was a way of wiping the slate clean, removing any shame, any disgrace from yourself." After the defeat of his remaining forces at Alexandria and hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony was the first of the two lovers to die by suicide.

According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, who based his account on that of Cleopatra's personal physician, Cleopatra visited Antony's tomb, bathed, ate and sent Octavian a sealed letter asking to be buried beside Antony, signaling that she meant to die. Octavian realized what was happening and sent messengers rushing to her, but they arrived too late. They found her dead in her royal regalia, with her attendants Iras and Charmion dying beside her.

A statue depicting Cleopatra's suicide by asp, the most famous of several ancient theories.

Jones has compiled what ancient historians, biographers, geographers and physicians wrote about Cleopatra's death. Every source mentions a snakebite, but several also suggest other possibilities, including a poisonous ointment, poison hidden in a hollow hairpin, and snake venom poured into a wound the queen made by biting herself. Only one of these writers, the geographer Strabo, was alive when Cleopatra died, and the only people in the room with her died, too.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio wrote that the sole clue was a pair of faint pricks on her arm. That doesn't settle much, however. "A cobra bite can appear as two small puncture wounds, but not all cobra bites appear this way and not all double puncture wounds result from snakebites," Jones said.

Jones traces the snake version of the story to Octavian, who was in Alexandria when Cleopatra died. Plutarch reported that an image of Cleopatra with an asp clinging to her was carried in Octavian's triumphal procession in Rome. "Octavian, however, was Cleopatra's enemy and for that reason we may not want to accept his account uncritically," Jones said.

Draycott suggested another possible source of confusion: Snake-shaped jewelry was fashionable in Alexandria at the time, so Romans viewing an effigy of the queen may have mistaken a snake bracelet for a real snake.

Draycott doesn't think one snake could have killed all three women. Jones is less certain. Snakes don't inject the same amount of venom with every bite, and some "dry bites" deliver none at all, Jones said. "On the other hand, I don't think it is impossible, as the body of a cobra contains enough venom to kill multiple people," she added.

The general view among historians, Draycott said, is that Cleopatra took some kind of poison — one that worked quickly and didn't cause seizures or vomiting. The absence of these symptoms is telling: An asp is believed to be what is now known as the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), whose venom causes a slow, agonizing death with respiratory failure.

A young Egyptian cobra (Naja haja) strikes a typical defensive pose in scrubland near Sidi Ifni, Morocco.

Cleopatra likely would have had other means, then. Alexandria was the Mediterranean's center of scientific study, and texts from the period, such as Nicander's "Theriaca," catalog venomous animals, Jones noted. Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, even consulted the pharmacologist Zopyrus about antidotes. Plutarch claimed that Cleopatra personally oversaw experiments that observed the effects of deadly poisons on condemned prisoners.

Still, that claim and other poison stories should be read with caution, Draycott said, because they draw on Roman stereotypes about women. In the Roman view, "manly men will battle with swords," while women, seen as "deceitful and weak" at this time, were thought to kill in secret. "They'll sneak it into your food," Draycott said, summing up the stereotype.

Roman writers were equally suspicious. Poisoning allegations dogged the Hellenistic dynasties of ancient Egypt and the neighboring Seleucid kingdom, as well as Rome's own imperial family. Some were probably true, Draycott said, but others may have been foodborne illnesses or other health conditions people didn't understand.

The method may remain a mystery, but for most historians, the motive doesn't change: Cleopatra chose to die on her own terms.

Olivia Maule is a former Live Science intern and science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

#6417. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

#6416. Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a big part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Earth is one big system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a new trick with them: photosynthesis.

Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

But this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

New research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations."

The oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

The researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research shows that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on new geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

They found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

The second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

The researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

This graphic illustrates the results from new research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that shows how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it shows that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life."

This figure shows the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

It all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work shows that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

The pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6415. This Dietary Supplement Could Have Potential Brain Benefits, Study Finds

A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising new questions about its potential benefits.

When the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients. For people with obesity, changes in blood vessel function can affect circulation, raising questions about how well the brain responds to these demands. A new clinical trial suggests a dietary supplement could help increase blood flow during mental activity, although researchers have yet to show that it improves memory.

Researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts. The amount people naturally produce varies, and existing research suggests that production declines with age and increasing body mass index. Urolithin A is also available as a dietary supplement.

In the randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA Network Open, 50 adults with obesity, ages 40 to 64, received either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A daily or a placebo for four weeks.

Participants taking the supplement showed a greater increase in blood flow to the brain while completing a challenging memory task. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area involved in holding and using information over short periods. However, researchers found no significant improvements in blood vessel function in the arm or performance on memory tests.

“The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity,” said first author Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.”

According to the researchers, this is the first human study to report an effect of urolithin A on blood vessel function in the brain. The supplement was well-tolerated, although the trial involved relatively few participants at a single research site. Longer studies with larger groups will be needed to determine whether the changes in blood flow lead to lasting health benefits.

“These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain,” said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. “Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.”

The researchers ultimately hope to find ways to help people maintain their cognitive health as they age.

“The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline,” Langley said. “We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.”

Reference: “Urolithin A and Endothelial and Cerebrovascular Function in Middle-Aged Adults With Obesity: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley, Rafal Gulej, Zalan Kaposzta, Zsofia Szarvas, Ali Shahriari, Henry Kinnard, Bryan Ticer, Camila B. Pinto, Peter Mukli, Mihaly Muranyi, Cheryl Adams, Jeng Kong, Leah Anderson, Stefano Tarantini, Yan Daniel Zhao, Norman G. Hord and Andriy Yabluchanskiy, 9 October 2026, JAMA Network Open. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38047

Research reported in this publication was supported by the American Heart Association (grant No. 24DIVSUP1282484 awarded to Dr da Costa Pinaffi-Langley) and the Reynolds Foundation.

#6414. Scientists Uncover a Natural Molecule That Makes Muscles Stronger and More Resistant to Fatigue

A molecule released during exercise could help muscles fight the weakness and fatigue that make staying active so difficult for many people with type 2 diabetes.

Exercise does more than burn calories and build strength. It triggers a complex series of chemical signals that help muscles become stronger, more efficient, and more resistant to fatigue. But for people with type 2 diabetes, muscle weakness and declining endurance can make it difficult to stay active, creating a cycle that may worsen their condition.

Researchers at the University of Leeds have identified a molecule that could help break that cycle. Known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), this naturally occurring compound acts as a key signal that helps muscles respond to exercise.

The researchers found that it plays an important role in reshaping muscle fibers, improving metabolism, and enhancing strength and endurance. It also helps protect muscles against damage and weakness associated with type 2 diabetes, raising the possibility of future treatments that preserve muscle function and make physical activity more manageable.

Published in Nature Communications, the research was led by Professor Lee Roberts and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBRSC).

Exercise prompts muscles to adapt so they can better handle future demands. Scientists are still investigating how the body coordinates these adaptations, and Roberts’ team wanted to understand whether those processes could inform treatments for chronic disease.

L-BAIBA was already known for its effects on metabolism. In research published in 2014, Roberts helped show that BAIBA could boost the fat-burning effects of exercise. L-BAIBA is now sold as a nutritional supplement, although the new findings concern its biological role and potential as a future treatment.

The latest study extends that earlier work by identifying L-BAIBA as a regulator of muscle remodeling. Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said, “Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

“This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes.”

L-BAIBA’s protective effects could be particularly valuable for people with type 2 diabetes, who can experience muscle loss, declining strength, and impaired metabolism. Weakness and fatigue can make exercise harder, creating a barrier to an activity that helps manage the condition. Future treatments targeting L-BAIBA could help people stay active by improving their muscles’ resistance to fatigue.

The need for better ways to manage type 2 diabetes is growing as the condition becomes more common among younger adults. Cases among people under 40 are now increasing faster than those among people over 40. The condition can lead to serious complications, including heart attacks and strokes, and develops through a complex mix of factors, with risk influenced by age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: “Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives.”

Reference: “The metabokine β-aminoisobutyric acid mediates exercise performance and skeletal muscle adaptation through a PGC1α-BAIBA-PPARδ axis” by Helene N. Daou, Nicole T. Watt, Shaimaa A. Gad, Amanda DV MacCannell, Aysha Ali, Chew Cheng, Raquel L. Fernando, T. Simon Futers, Sumeet A. Khetarpal, Harrison Gallagher, Luis D. Chinait, Anselmo S. Moriscot, Pim Knuiman, Koen Manusama, Marco Mensink, Irvin Teh, Jurgen E. Schneider, Richard Cubbon, Guy S. Taylor, Daniel J. West, David J. Beech, T. Scott Bowen and Lee D. Roberts, 18 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76307-8

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#6412. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

This story was updated on November 13, 2026, to correct the spelling of Katy Croff Bell's name, and to correct the location of the corals mentioned in the story from the Indian to the Pacific Ocean.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6411. A Study of 50,000 Children Reveals the Real Impact of Daily Iron Pills

A major scientific review involving more than 50,000 children and adolescents reveals that daily iron supplementation can significantly reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia.

A daily iron supplement can substantially reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia in children and teenagers, but it does not appear to improve growth or protect against common illnesses. These findings come from a major Cochrane review of 114 studies involving more than 50,000 participants.

Led by researchers at Cornell University’s Joan Klein Jacobs Center for Precision Nutrition and Health, the review examined daily iron supplements taken alone or combined with folic acid and other vitamins and minerals. Many of the studies were conducted in Asia and involved children younger than five.

The strongest evidence showed that iron alone probably reduces the risk of iron deficiency anemia compared with receiving no treatment or a placebo. Combining iron with folic acid probably offers similar protection, although that conclusion was based on just one study. Supplements containing iron alongside other vitamins and minerals may also help. Evidence suggests that iron supplementation can reduce anemia and iron deficiency more broadly, but confidence in several findings remains limited.

Iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen from the lungs throughout the body. When iron levels become too low, the body cannot produce enough healthy hemoglobin, potentially leading to iron deficiency anemia.

“Iron deficiency remains one of the most common nutritional problems affecting children worldwide,” says first author Dr Kripa Rajagopalan. “Our review shows that daily iron supplements do what they are meant to do, which is reduce iron deficiency anemia, without any measurable impact on the common illnesses parents and health workers worry about.”

Although iron supplements helped prevent iron deficiency anemia, the researchers found no improvement in children’s height or weight relative to others of the same age and sex. Iron alone also had no measurable effect on the occurrence of cough, fever, or respiratory illness.

Adding folic acid to iron made little to no difference in rates of diarrhea or respiratory illness. Results for other supplement combinations were less conclusive, with evidence ranging from moderate to very low certainty.

Daily iron supplementation may cause stool discoloration, but iron alone appears to have little or no effect on vomiting or diarrhea. Its relationship with constipation remains uncertain. When iron was included in supplements containing other vitamins and minerals, vomiting was probably more common than with otherwise identical supplements that lacked iron.

“While the evidence base supports the use of daily iron supplements where needed, some adverse effects do occur. Stool discoloration and, in some formulations, vomiting were more common with iron, and the certainty of evidence for several outcomes, including anemia and iron deficiency themselves, was low or very low,” explains senior author Dr Saurabh Mehta.

Uncertainty about longer-term outcomes has persisted for years. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, last updated in 2016, identified gaps in evidence concerning the long-term effects of iron supplementation in children. The new review brings together a much larger body of research, although the strength of the evidence still varies across outcomes.

Anemia affects an estimated 874 million children and women worldwide. Young children face a particularly heavy burden, with approximately 40% of children younger than five affected in 2019. Iron deficiency accounts for roughly half of these cases.

Preventing anemia is a central objective of the global health strategy for women, children, and adolescents through 2030. Iron supplementation is already widely used to prevent and treat anemia, particularly among adolescents and women in populations where iron deficiency is common.

“These findings give decision-makers a stronger evidence base for guidance on iron supplementation in children and adolescents,” says co-author Dr Julia L. Finkelstein. “The data supports continued use of iron supplementation where iron deficiency is a concern.”

The researchers caution that their findings do not justify giving every child or adolescent a daily iron tablet. Decisions about supplementation should account for individual nutritional needs, local rates of iron deficiency and anemia, and the specific supplement formulation being used.

Reference: “Daily iron supplementation for prevention or treatment of iron‐deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and adolescents” by Kripa Rajagopalan, Laura Hackl, Juan Pablo Peña-Rosas, Maria Nieves Garcia-Casal, Mochammad Rizal, Neel H Mehta, Michael Roudik, Saiful Islam, Meghan M Trumbull-Kennedy, Nabila Reem Khondakar, Juan VA Franco, Julia L Finkelstein and Saurabh Mehta, 17 November 2026, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD013227.pub2

#6410. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6409. Scientists X-Ray a Narwhal Tusk and Discover Something Extraordinary

Scientists are uncovering the secrets of narwhal tusks, revealing an unusual internal structure and new possibilities for studying decades of environmental change in the Arctic.

In the 17th century, King Frederik III of Denmark had a throne made entirely from unicorn horns. The extraordinary royal treasure came from an expedition he sent to Greenland, where the king knew the precious horns could be traced to a very real animal. It lived in Arctic waters, had fins instead of hooves, and was known as the narwhal. The expedition was a success, bringing the Danish ruler a throne that became a symbol of prestige and power across Europe. Yet the legendary horn was not a horn at all. It was a tooth.

And what a peculiar tooth it is. Unlike the curved tusks of elephants and walruses or the incisors of beavers, the male narwhal’s tusk grows forward in an elegant spiral. Usually, it is the left upper canine that extends through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it reaches lengths of up to two meters (6.6 feet), sometimes half the animal’s body length.

That unusual shape has fascinated scientists for years. Now, an international research team has uncovered something remarkable inside the tusk. Its microscopic building blocks form two intertwined spirals that twist in opposite directions, creating a structure that helps the enormous tooth withstand mechanical stress. The findings, published in Nature Communications, offer a new explanation for the anatomy behind one of nature’s most recognizable features.

For all their fame, narwhal tusks still hold plenty of mysteries. Scientists do not know exactly how the animals use them, although evidence suggests they play an important role in mate selection and social interaction. Narwhals have occasionally been observed engaging in playful tusk duels, further supporting a possible connection to reproduction and social behavior. The tusks also continue growing throughout the animal’s life and can themselves reach 70 years of age.

Understanding how such a long, spiraling tooth remains strong requires looking far beneath its surface. “Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth,” says Marianne Liebi, a researcher at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) and co-author of the study.

Most of the tusk consists of dentine, the same material that forms the core of human teeth. A thinner outer layer called cementum covers it, although in most other mammals, this tissue is normally found only around the tooth’s root. Both materials contain collagen fibers reinforced with tiny mineral crystals, combining flexibility with hardness.

The arrangement works somewhat like reinforced concrete. In buildings, concrete withstands compression while a steel framework provides strength against pulling forces. In the narwhal’s tooth, collagen fibers serve as internal reinforcement, while mineral crystals provide hardness. “The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible,” Liebi explains. “Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates.”

The challenge for the researchers was finding out how these microscopic materials relate to the enormous spiral visible from the outside.

“The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths,” Liebi explains.

To connect these vastly different scales, the team turned to a specialized X-ray technique called tensor tomography. Unlike an ordinary dental X-ray, which produces an image based on how strongly tissues absorb radiation, this method uses patterns created when powerful X-rays scatter from regularly arranged structures inside a material.

“From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented,” explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo, who joined the project as a PhD student at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and later continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

The researchers conducted their investigations at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at PSI in Villigen, Switzerland, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund, Sweden, and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in Grenoble, France. These facilities produce the powerful X-rays needed to examine extremely small structures.

During tensor tomography, the tooth is rotated within the X-ray beam and scanned point by point. Millions of measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional picture of its internal architecture, connecting the orientation of nanoscale fibers with the structure of the entire tooth.

After collecting this enormous amount of data, however, the scientists encountered an unexpected problem. The spiral they were searching for appeared to be missing.

“That puzzled us quite a bit,” Liebi recalls. Earlier mechanical tests had suggested that the tusk’s distinctive shape should already be reflected in the arrangement of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals. “But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern.”

The answer emerged when the researchers changed how they examined the data. Rather than concentrating on individual points within the three-dimensional images, they began comparing how those points were oriented relative to one another.

“When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear,” recalls Rodriguez-Palomo. “All we had to do then was connect the dots – as in a children’s paint-by-numbers kit – and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals.”

The outer cementum layer followed a left-handed helix, while the mineralized collagen structures within the dentine twisted in the opposite direction. Together, these interlocking spirals create an unusually stable architecture, much like the twisted strands of a rope. Their opposing orientations help the tooth resist twisting forces and other mechanical stresses while contributing to its distinctive external spiral.

The researchers are also interested in another remarkable property of narwhal tusks: their ability to preserve a record of the Arctic environment.

Led by Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international team is investigating how tusk growth relates to environmental and climate conditions. Much like the annual rings of a tree, the growth structures within a narwhal’s tooth can provide clues about past conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

Because the tusk grows continuously, it can preserve environmental information across much of an animal’s life, which can approach a century. A tooth once mistaken for evidence of a mythical creature may therefore also hold a decades-long record of life in the Arctic.

Reference: “The narwhal tusk assembles its macroscopic helix from building blocks with opposing twists” by Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo, Peter Alling Strange Vibe, Dimitra Athanasiadou, Jonas Palle, Leonard C. Nielsen, Jonathan T. Avaro, Thorbjørn Erik Køppen Christensen, Nina Kølln Wittig, Mads Ry Vogel Jørgensen, Innokenty Kantor, Manfred Burghammer, Jiliang Liu, Stefano Checchia, Christian Appel, Karl Anker Jørgensen, Eva Garde, Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen, Marianne Liebi and Henrik Birkedal, 18 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75689-z

The study is part of the NordForsk-funded research project “Narwhal tusks – a tale with a twist.” It was supported by the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie program.

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

#6407. Scientists Just Challenged a Decades-Old Belief About How Cells Work

The tools scientists use to study cells may be changing the very proteins they observe, raising questions about decades of research into how cells maintain their structure.

For decades, textbooks and hundreds of scientific papers have described coronin proteins as important organizers of the internal framework that gives cells their shape and helps them move. Now, researchers at the University of Basel in Switzerland are revisiting that longstanding explanation, showing how scientific progress can sometimes begin by questioning what we thought we already knew.

Coronins are found in organisms ranging from single-celled amoebae to humans. They are involved in essential processes such as immunity, development, and cell survival. Scientists have traditionally viewed them as proteins that interact with actin, a major component of the cytoskeleton. This network of tiny filaments supports a cell’s structure, allows it to move, and helps organize its contents.

A new study published in PLOS Biology, led by Professor Jean Pieters at the University of Basel’s Biozentrum, challenges that understanding. Using a broad range of experiments to examine coronins in their natural state, the researchers found that these proteins are largely unnecessary for the overall organization of the actin cytoskeleton.

“Over the years, my laboratory failed to find evidence for a direct role of coronin proteins in actin binding and modulation across a wide range of model systems,” says Pieters. “Even cells lacking coronins continue to organize and remodel their actin networks normally. Of course, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.”

The team also identified a possible reason why earlier studies reached different conclusions. To observe proteins inside living cells, scientists often attach molecular tags that make them easier to track. Although these tools are widely used, they can sometimes interfere with the proteins being studied.

“These tags are extremely useful and assumed to be innocuous for protein function,” says Roko Gvozdenica, the study’s first author. “However, we found that the tagging of coronin proteins has the potential to cause loss of their function and significantly alter their localization.”

This raises the possibility that some earlier evidence linking coronins to actin resulted from experimental artifacts rather than their natural behavior. The researchers also found that many antibodies used to detect coronins lack specificity, adding to broader concerns about the reliability of these tools in biomedical research.

The findings bring attention to another important role of coronins: helping cells communicate through chemical signals.

“Over the years, we have reported that coronins are involved in cell signaling,” emphasizes Pieters. “In the immune system, for example, coronin involvement in these signaling processes was found to be essential for the maintenance of normal T cell numbers, which is vital for protecting the body against infections or cancer.”

The researchers caution that their findings do not completely rule out a connection between coronins and the cytoskeleton. These proteins may still influence its organization, either directly or indirectly through cell signaling.

By reexamining an idea that has shaped research for decades, the study opens new possibilities for understanding how coronins help cells communicate, survive, and maintain healthy cell numbers.

Reference: “Reassessment of the roles of coronin proteins as actin effectors and in signaling” by Roko Gvozdenica Šipić, Haiyan Zhang, Andrii Kharin, Jerneja Koren, Viviana D’Otolo, Yuko Nariai, Takeshi Urano, Pawel Pelczar, Klemens Fröhlich, Alexander Schmidt, Urszula Brykczynska Kunzmann, Tohnyui Ndinyanka Fabrice, Alexey Baldin and Jean Pieters, 18 August 2026, PLOS Biology. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003904
